details:
MYG-351: Last Signal is a 14-day, single-player 2D management simulator set in the Artemis-MYG lunar mission (year 2032). The player is Elena, commander of the Orion spacecraft, and must bring four astronauts back to Earth, each with their own character: Elena, Marcus (systems engineer), Sofía (physician) and Leo (mechanical engineer). Before launch, the player splits 10,000 mission credits between two equipment packages: one focused on survival and the other on science and propulsion. Each package changes the numbers for the whole run.

Over the 14 days, the ship consumes water, food, oxygen and electricity on its own. Every day the player makes two timed decisions: an emergency (oxygen leaks, solar storms, electrical failures) and a resource-management decision. If time runs out, the crew acts on its own, almost always worse. The result of each decision depends on the chosen option, the ship's state and the crew's stress, so the same decision can turn out differently on different days. There are 65 decisions, 3 possible endings (mission accomplished, mission aborted and total silence) and a final score.

Benefits and impact: the game teaches hands-on that in space no option is free, that resources are limited and that decisions have delayed consequences. After each decision it explains what happened, why it happened and what the other options would have done, with memos based on NASA references on life support, radiation, water and CO₂. It is meant to introduce students to resource management and decision-making under pressure.

Tools: Godot 4 with GDScript, pixel-art graphics and real NASA data, such as 2.5 L of water per astronaut per day and 3,035 kcal per person. We used AI tools to help us program the game, to create some of the scripts and to generate the audio. The game design, story and rules were defined by our team, who reviewed and tested the results. The game is available in English and Spanish, with a language selector in the menu.

Source code: https://github.com/GiovannyBatista/Reto-de-la-nasa

Creativity: it combines a "build your ship" budget with timed crises. Each crew member's stress generates its own events according to their character, and manual repair minigames change the outcome of emergencies.

Team factors: balancing survival and science, making sure no option is obviously correct, fidelity to real data, clarity for new players and replayability.
